kits.familyName: An easy change with wider effects
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. A {client} asks you to change how their {deliverable} is handled, and the change would be easy for you.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you get a request from a {client} for a small change in how their {deliverable} is handled.
pressure: The {client} says other places do it this way without any fuss.
{coworker3} says to just do it and keep the {client} happy.
detail: The {client} has been coming here for years.
The request came in by phone.

tiers.1: A step that protects people outweighs convenience.
tiers.2: The person the organization assigns to decide has to decide.
tiers.3: The teams down the line need a say before their work changes.
tiers.4: Flagging a possible precedent comes after the decision itself is in the right hands.
tiers.5: Explaining the reason helps once the bigger questions are settled.

fact: The change would skip a step that exists to protect {client.plural}.
issues.action: Explain that the step protects {client.plural}, and offer an option that keeps it.
issues.brief: keep the protective step and offer an option
issues.reason: The step exists for everyone's protection. Offering an alternative meets the {client}'s need without removing it.
issues.lesson: Weigh a request against the purpose of the steps it would change.

shortcut.text: Skip the step just for this {client}, since it is only one order.
shortcut.brief: skip it for this one order
shortcut.why: The protection matters on every order. One exception can be the one that goes wrong.
shortcut.mis: A single exception has no wider effect.

fact: The posted chart of responsibilities says {lead|the} decides changes like this.
clear: {Lead|the} already approved changes like this one last week.
issues.done: changes like this were already approved
issues.action: Pass the request to {lead|the}, who decides changes like this.
issues.reason: Knowing who decides what is part of understanding how the organization works. It keeps decisions consistent.
issues.lesson: Know who is responsible for which decisions, and route requests to them.

shortcut.text: Make the change yourself, since you are the one the {client} asked.
shortcut.why: Being asked does not give you authority. The chart says the lead decides.
shortcut.mis: Whoever gets a request can decide it.

fact: The change would add work for the team that handles the next step.
clear: The next team already said the change works for them.
issues.short: the extra work for the next team
issues.action: Check with the next team about the extra work before agreeing.
issues.reason: A change that is easy for you may be hard for the team after you. Checking first avoids surprising them.
issues.lesson: Think about how your actions affect the people who work after you.

shortcut.text: Agree to the change, since it does not make your own job harder.
shortcut.brief: agree since it is easy for you
shortcut.why: Judging a change only by your own work ignores its effect on the next team.
shortcut.mis: If it is easy for you, it is easy for everyone.

fact: If the change is made, other {client.plural} are likely to ask for the same thing.
issues.short: the precedent the change would set
issues.action: Tell {lead|the} that making this change may lead others to expect it too.
issues.reason: Decisions often repeat. Flagging the wider effect helps the lead decide with the full picture.
issues.lesson: Consider whether a one-time decision will become an expectation.

shortcut.text: Ignore that, since you can deal with other requests when they come.
shortcut.why: Once a change is made for one {client}, refusing others becomes harder.

clear: {Lead|the} already knows other {client.plural} may ask for the same change.
issues.done: the lead already knows about the precedent

proceed.text: Make the change for the {client} and note it in {record|the}.
proceed.why: The change is approved, others are on board and nothing is put at risk, so making and recording it is right.
proceed.lesson: When a change is approved and its effects are understood, carry it out and record it.

generic.text: Tell the {client} no without explaining why.
generic.why: A flat refusal with no explanation leaves the {client} confused and unhappy.

generic.text: Promise the {client} the change before checking anything.
generic.why: Promising first may commit the workplace to something it cannot or should not do.
generic.mis: A promise can always be undone later.

overcaution.text: Ask every department to review the change before you do anything.
overcaution.why: The change is already approved and agreed. A full review is unnecessary.
overcaution.mis: More reviews always make a decision better.

setup: A {client} at {workplace|the} has asked for a change in how their {deliverable} is handled.

authority: The chart of responsibilities assigns this kind of decision to {lead|the}.
downstream: Another team handles the step after yours.

steps.text: Find out exactly what the {client} wants changed
Ask the next team how it affects them
Bring the request to {lead|the} for a decision

rel: You need the details before asking about the effect.
The lead needs the details to decide.
The decision should include the next team's view.
The {client} hears the outcome after the decision.
You respond after understanding the request.
process.lesson: Understand the request, gather the affected views, let the right person decide, then follow through.

title: Your reply to the {client}
intro: You are about to reply to the {client}'s request. Check the message first.
doc.lesson: Big-picture replies explain decisions in terms of their purpose and route them to the right people.

lines.text: Thank you for your request about how your {deliverable} is handled.
The extra check you asked us to skip is there to protect every {client}.
lines.fine: Explains the purpose of the step.

lines.text: We can instead have your order ready an hour earlier.
lines.fine: Offers an alternative that keeps the check.

bad.text: So we will skip that check for your orders from now on.
bad.why: The same message says the check protects every {client}. Dropping it contradicts that reason.

lines.text: I have passed your request to {lead|the}, who makes these decisions.
lines.fine: Routes the decision to the right person.

bad.text: I have decided to change our process for everyone starting today.
bad.why: Changing the process for everyone is not an individual's decision; it belongs to the person responsible.

lines.text: You will hear back by Friday.

bad.text: We will get back to you whenever someone has time.
bad.why: A vague promise leaves the {client} unsure when to expect an answer.

bad.text: Please stop asking for special treatment.
bad.why: This is rude and damages the relationship with the {client}.

review.notes: Organization structure stated via a posted chart of responsibilities.

kits.familyName: Small closing habits with wider effects
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}, and you are the last one closing up tonight.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are finishing the closing routine on your own.
detail: It has been a long day.
Everyone else left about ten minutes ago.

fact: Trash bags by the back door are spilling onto the sidewalk, and {workplace|the} promised neighbors to keep trash in closed bins.
issues.action: Put the trash in the closed bins, keeping the promise made to the neighbors.
issues.reason: The workplace's reputation in the neighborhood depends on keeping its promises. A few minutes now protects that relationship.
issues.lesson: Your everyday actions shape how the community sees your workplace.

shortcut.text: Leave the bags for the morning crew, since it is late.
shortcut.why: Overnight, the trash stays on the sidewalk and breaks the promise to neighbors.
shortcut.mis: Small messes outside do not affect the business.

fact: {Powered|the} is still running in an empty room, and the closing list says it should be off overnight.
issues.action: Switch off {powered|the} using the normal shutdown steps.
issues.reason: Leaving equipment on wastes energy and money and adds wear. The closing list exists because those costs add up.
issues.lesson: Small wastes repeated every night become big costs for the organization.

shortcut.text: Leave it on, since one night of power costs almost nothing.
shortcut.why: Habits repeat. One night becomes every night, and the cost adds up.
shortcut.mis: Small costs do not matter to a business.

fact: A sealed box of unused {supply.plural} has been thrown in the trash.
issues.short: the sealed box in the trash
issues.action: Take the sealed box out of the trash and return it to the supply shelf.
issues.reason: Unused supplies cost money to replace. Returning them protects the budget everyone depends on.
issues.lesson: Treat the organization's resources as if your own budget depended on them.

shortcut.text: Leave it, since someone must have had a reason to throw it out.
shortcut.why: A sealed, unused box has value. If there is a reason, it can be checked tomorrow.
shortcut.mis: Whatever is in the trash must be waste.

fact: This is the third night this week the closing list has been left half done.
issues.action: Finish the list, then let {lead|the} know it keeps happening so the routine can be fixed.
issues.reason: Fixing tonight's gaps helps once. Telling the lead about the pattern helps fix the routine for every night.
issues.lesson: Look beyond the single incident to the pattern behind it.

shortcut.text: Finish the list again and say nothing, since it is easier.
shortcut.why: Quietly covering a repeated gap leaves the cause in place.
shortcut.mis: Covering a problem is the same as solving it.

proceed.text: Lock up and head home, since tonight's closing is someone else's job.
proceed.why: Closing is your responsibility tonight, so leaving things undone is not an option.
proceed.lesson: Every closing task protects something bigger than the task itself.

generic.text: Write a note about it and leave everything as it is.
generic.why: A note does not fix a problem you can handle in minutes.
generic.mis: Writing a note is the same as handling it.

generic.text: Text {coworker} to come back and handle it.
generic.why: You are the one closing. Calling someone back is not necessary for a task you can do.
generic.mis: Closing problems belong to whoever caused them.

review.notes: Beginner-only issues; the promise to neighbors and the closing list are stated in the scenario.

setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Lead|the} asked you to look into switching to a cheaper supplier for {supply.plural}.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are comparing the current supplier of {supply.plural} with a cheaper one for {lead|the}.
pressure: {coworker3} says cheaper is always better and to just switch.
detail: The cheaper supplier sent free samples.
The current supplier has been used for years.

tiers.1: A safety concern stops the change until it is resolved.
tiers.2: Commitments the workplace already made have to be checked before changing.
tiers.3: The people whose work changes need a say.
tiers.4: A fair comparison needs the full cost.
tiers.5: Wider effects belong in the summary once the facts are in.

fact: The cheaper {supply.plural} failed a safety test at another workplace.
issues.action: Report the failed safety test to {lead|the} before the switch goes further.
issues.reason: A cheaper product that may be unsafe could cost far more than it saves.

shortcut.text: Switch anyway, since the test was at a different workplace.
shortcut.why: A failed test elsewhere is a warning the lead needs to hear.
shortcut.mis: Problems elsewhere do not apply here.

fact: The agreement with the current supplier, kept by {lead|the}, may require notice before switching.
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} to check the agreement before anything changes.
issues.reason: Breaking an agreement can cost money and trust. The lead holds the agreement.
issues.lesson: Check existing commitments before changing course.

shortcut.text: Assume the agreement does not matter, since the switch saves money.
shortcut.why: Savings do not cancel a commitment the workplace made.
shortcut.mis: Agreements do not matter if money is saved.

clear: {Lead|the} checked, and the agreement allows switching at any time.

fact: The cheaper version would mean the next team changes how they work.
issues.short: the effect on the next team
issues.action: Ask the next team how the change would affect their work.
issues.brief: ask the next team about the effect
issues.reason: Savings in one place can create costs in another. The next team knows their side.
issues.lesson: Look at how a change affects the whole operation.

shortcut.text: Leave them out, since purchasing is not their job.
shortcut.why: They will live with the change; leaving them out risks hidden costs.

clear: The next team tested the samples and said they work fine.
issues.done: the next team already tested the samples

fact: The cheaper price does not include shipping, which the current supplier covers.
issues.action: Compare the total cost with shipping included, not just the price.
issues.reason: A lower price can become a higher total once all costs are counted.
issues.lesson: Compare total costs, not sticker prices.

shortcut.text: Compare the prices only, since shipping is a small extra.
shortcut.mis: Extra costs are too small to matter.

clear: You already compared both options with shipping included.
issues.done: the full costs were already compared

fact: The current supplier is a local business that many {client.plural} know.
issues.action: Mention the local relationship in your summary for {lead|the}.
issues.reason: Community relationships affect reputation. The lead should weigh them with the numbers.
issues.lesson: Consider how decisions affect the community.

shortcut.text: Leave it out, since only the price matters.
shortcut.why: Leaving out a real factor gives the lead an incomplete picture.
shortcut.mis: Business decisions are only about price.

proceed.text: Recommend the option that comes out best, with your comparison, to {lead|the}.
proceed.why: The facts are in and nothing blocks a decision, so a clear recommendation is the next step.
proceed.lesson: Recommend a change once its effects across the organization are understood.

generic.text: Switch suppliers yourself today to save time.
generic.why: The lead asked for a recommendation, not a decision.
generic.mis: Being asked to look into something means you decide.

generic.text: Tell {lead|the} the current supplier is fine without looking further.
generic.why: Skipping the comparison leaves the lead without the information requested.
generic.mis: Keeping things the same never needs a reason.

overcaution.text: Ask for three more months to study the options.
overcaution.why: The facts are already in; more delay adds no value.
overcaution.mis: More study always improves a decision.

setup: {Lead|the} at {workplace|the} asked you to compare a cheaper supplier of {supply.plural} with the current one.

contract: The current supplier agreement may have conditions.
nextteam: Another team uses these supplies after you.
shipping: The two suppliers handle shipping differently.

steps.text: Ask the next team to test samples
Add up the total cost of each option
Compare the options side by side

rel: The recommendation depends on whether switching is allowed.
The comparison needs the next team's results.
process.lesson: Check commitments, gather affected views and full costs, compare, then recommend.

title: Supplier comparison for {lead|the}
intro: Check your supplier comparison before sending it.
doc.lesson: A big-picture recommendation counts safety, commitments, other teams, full cost and community effects.

lines.text: Price: the new supplier is 12 percent cheaper per item.
Shipping: the new supplier adds a fee; the total saving is 4 percent.

bad.why: Leaving out shipping can hide costs that erase the savings.

lines.text: The next team tested samples and found no problems.

bad.text: The next team was not asked, since it is not their decision.
bad.why: The team that uses the supplies should be consulted.

lines.text: The current agreement allows switching with 30 days' notice.
The current supplier is a long-time local business.
Recommendation: switch after giving 30 days' notice.

bad.why: The agreement requires 30 days' notice, so switching tomorrow breaks it.

review.notes: Agreement terms are stated as facts in the scenario; no legal claims.
